fetched_contents.text: Designing biochar through controlled synthesis: Correlating processing conditions with functional performance 1. Introduction Biochar is a carbon-rich solid obtained through the carbonization of biomass, such as wood, crop residues, or plant leaves [1], [2]. Owing to its versatility, biochar is widely used as an efficient adsorbent for heavy metals and organic contaminants in water and soil [3], for greenhouse gases in the atmosphere [4], as a slow-release fertilizer [3], and anaerobic fermentation support for methane or hydrogen production [5]. The physicochemical properties of biochar are strongly influenced by feedstock and the production method, with thermochemical techniques (pyrolysis, gasification, torrefaction, hydrothermal, and flash carbonization) shaping structural and chemical characteristics according to process conditions [6], and feedstock composition affecting surface chemistry and overall material performance [7]. Several reviews [8], [9], [10] have investigated in the past how synthesis parameters (e.g., feedstock composition and temperature) influence the physicochemical properties of biochar (such as porosity, surface chemistry, and adsorption capacity). While these works provide valuable descriptive correlations, they largely lack conceptual design frameworks for designing biochars with tailored functionalities. Furthermore, previous studies [11] often focus on post-synthesis modification to adapt biochars suitable for specific applications, rather than guiding the selection of synthesis parameters to produce functionally optimized materials from the outset. To address these gaps, this review proposes a design-oriented and qualitatively predictive approach that systematically links synthesis conditions, structural features, and functional performance, culminating in a conceptual design framework to guide the selection and engineering of biochars with physicochemical properties tailored to specific technological applications. The literature considered in this review was identified through searches in major scientific databases, including Google Scholar, and Scopus. Searches were performed using combinations of keywords related to biochar synthesis, feedstock composition, pyrolysis conditions, physicochemical properties, and application domains. Particular attention was given to studies investigating the relationships between feedstock characteristics, synthesis parameters, physicochemical properties, and functional performance of biochar, which form the conceptual basis of the framework proposed in this review. Priority was given to recent publications, while also considering earlier studies that have significantly contributed to the understanding of biochar synthesis and functionality. 2. Pyrolysis Pyrolysis is one of the most widely employed thermochemical processes for biochar synthesis. Its widespread use is mainly due to its ability, under oxygen-limited conditions and appropriate operating parameters, to favour the formation of a solid carbonaceous fraction while generating gaseous and condensable co-products. The relative distribution of these products is strongly dependent on factors such as reactor configuration, heating rate, peak temperature, residence time, and feedstock composition. Moreover, pyrolysis allows a high degree of flexibility in tuning operational parameters, such as heating rate, peak temperature, and residence time, enabling precise control over the resulting physicochemical properties of biochar. In many commonly used laboratory-scale and industrial configurations, pyrolysis processes are optimized to favor biochar production, while the gaseous and condensable fractions can be recovered as byproducts and potentially valorized for energy generation or further processing. Compared with other thermochemical conversion processes, pyrolysis is often considered particularly suitable for biochar production due to its operational flexibility, potential scalability, and the possibility of achieving relatively favorable energy balances depending on reactor design and process integration, making it a commonly adopted approach for the development of engineered biochars with tailored functionalities. In the following paragraphs, the main features of the pyrolysis process are first introduced, followed by a discussion of how operational parameters influence biochar properties and, finally, an overview of the different pyrolysis regimes. Pyrolysis is a thermochemical process in which biomass is heated in the absence or limited amount of oxygen under atmospheric pressure, between 300 and 900 °C [1]. During this process, biomass is converted into different products, including non-condensable gases (pyrogas), liquid fractions (biocrude or bio-oil), and a solid carbonaceous residue, known as biochar. The relative yield of these products mainly depends on reaction temperature, heating rate, and residence time [12]. Biochar yield and the abundance of acidic surface functional groups (i.e., carboxyl and phenolic groups) usually decrease with increasing temperature, whereas basic functional groups (i.e., amino and pyridinic-N groups [13]), ash content, pH, and carbon stability tend to increase [1]. At the same time, non-volatile inorganic elements (i.e., Ca, Mg [14]) become progressively enriched in the biochar matrix [15]. From a practical perspective, the influence of temperature on biochar properties can be broadly interpreted as follows [16]: (i) at relatively low temperatures (300–500 °C), biochars typically retain a higher abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups; (ii) at intermediate temperatures (500–700 °C), devolatilization processes promote the progressive development of porosity and surface area; (iii) at higher temperatures (>700 °C), further aromatization and structural rearrangements may occur, sometimes leading to partial sintering of the carbon matrix. fetched_contents.text: Three-year field experiments revealed the immobilization effect of natural aging biochar on typical heavy metals (Pb, Cu, Cd) Introduction In recent years, it has been well demonstrated that biochar, a solid residue pyrolyzed from waste biomass under oxygen-limited conditions (Sohi et al., 2010), could efficiently immobilize heavy metals in soil owning to its characteristics of alkalinity, ash content, high porous structure, and surface functional groups (Fan et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2017). Whereas once applicated in the soil, biochar may undergo an aging process. Various natural factors including freeze-thaw cycles, wetting-drying cycles, biotic and abiotic redox reactions, solubilization or interaction with microbes and minerals may be all involved in biochar aging over time in the field (Xu et al., 2018). As a result, biochar may suffer long-term significant changes in physicochemical properties, such as the specific surface area (SSA), acidity, elemental composition, functional group, ion exchange capacity, and the aromaticity (Jing et al., 2020), which in turn influences its performance in immobilizing heavy metals. Quite a few studies verified that aged biochar had an enhanced capacity of metal sorption (Pb2+, Cd2+, Cu2+, Zn2+) because of the accessibility of biochar's pore network and reactive surfaces (Rechberger et al., 2019), the increased active sorption sites (Fan et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2022) and oxygenated functional groups (Tan et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022). While Guo et al. (2014) reported the opposite results that the adsorption capacity of Cu(II) on aging rice husk biochar decreased. Tan et al. (2020) also found that aging could lead to SSA changes of biochar and then the changes of Pb adsorption. Through 2-year field investigation of several metal(loid)s on various biochar aging in different soils, Campos et al. (2021) argued that aging might enhance or decrease the adsorption of metal(loid)s, which varied among tested metal(loid)s, biochar and soils. As a consequence, we could deduce that the following aspects need further exploration, which are all imperative for biochar in remediating metal contaminated soils. Firstly, long-term field experiment concerning biochar aging is still needed. It is time-consuming to monitor the long-term natural aging of biochar in the field, because some natural aging process is very slow (Spokas, 2010). Therefore, various simulated aging methods under controlled laboratory conditions, including chemical oxidation, physical aging, biological aging and/or with several methods combined, have been tested to accelerate the aging process (Fan et al., 2018; Meng et al., 2022a; Tan et al., 2020). However, drastic discrepancy may exist between simulated aging and natural aging, because multiple environmental factors such as water condition, climatic change, biological activities, redox cycles etc., all affect biochar aging in the field (Wang et al., 2020). Up to date, the information on biochar natural long-term aging is limited, still less in the field with multi-contaminated metals (Campos et al., 2021). Secondly, the stability of immobilized metals on biochar in soils should be considered. The sorption ability of biochar after aging has aroused the study attention (Fan et al., 2018; Meng et al., 2022a; Mia et al., 2017a; Tan et al., 2020), while most the studies centered at the sorption performance of aged biochar, the information of desorption risk of the immobilized metals is scarce, especially the desorption of immobilized metals from biochar under remediation soils in the long term. To the best of our knowledge, only Meng et al. (2022a) studied the desorption of Cd, Ni, and Cu on simulated aged soil and biochar. Thirdly, the conflicting results still exist in the effect of biochar aging on metal immobilization, and further investigation is necessary about the release risk of metals immobilized by biochar under changing field conditions. In this study, the stability of immobilized heavy metals (Cd, Cu, Pb) on biochar during a 3-year remediation for soil in the field was investigated. Desorption experiments were conducted to explore the release risk of immobilized metals during long-term field remediation process. Because soil properties, especially pH and dissolved organic matter (DOC), might change owning to acid rain, plant roots, and the activities of microbes (Jiang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2020; Jones, 1998), the immobilized metals might release into soil solution again under the long-term remediation process. So, different pH values were set in the desorption experiment to simulate the variance of pH such as acid rain circumstance. Here we tested the hypothesis that field aging of biochar may exhibit some difference from those in simulated aging, and thus different metal immobilization effect. We also sought to find out whether biochar can continuously reduce the availability of Cd, Cu and Pb in soils. The main objectives of our study were 1) to identify the release risk of Cd, Cu, Pb from biochar remediated soils under different field pH conditions; 2) to reveal the behind mechanisms governing the stability of fixed metals through the characterization of biochar under long-term aging in the field; 3) to comprehensively evaluate the practical repair efficacy of biochar in multiple-metal polluted soils. The results are anticipated to improve our understanding of the relationship between physicochemical changes on biochar under field aging and the efficacy of biochar-assisted repair for multiple-metal contaminated soils. Biochar’s metal-ion adsorption is driven by a combination of mechanisms, with the strongest evidence pointing to surface complexation, ion exchange, electrostatic attraction, and sometimes surface precipitation. The search evidence explicitly lists major physicochemical sorption processes as surface sorption, electrostatic attraction, surface complexation, precipitation, and ion exchange [N2-R3]. Another source expands this by mentioning adsorption mechanisms including pore filling, electrostatic adsorption, π–π interactions, ion exchange, and mineral formation [N2-R1], while a more specific metal-sorption review similarly identifies surface complexation, ion exchange, and precipitation as central processes [N2-R3]. A Cd-specific example also points to precipitation, ion exchange, functional group complexation, and cation-π interactions [N2-R4]. Taken together, these sources support the conclusion that multiple mechanisms operate simultaneously, and the dominant ones for metal adsorption onto biochar are surface complexation, ion exchange, electrostatic attraction, and precipitation [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

The functional group density and chemistry strongly influence binding affinity and capacity. The search evidence directly states that biochar adsorption performance is strongly correlated with the diversity and abundance of surface oxygen-containing functional groups, particularly [N1-R2]. Another source notes that the abundance of acidic surface functional groups, such as carboxyl and phenolic groups, usually decreases with increasing pyrolysis temperature, whereas basic functional groups increase [N1-F1]. This implies that functional group density is not static: higher oxygen-containing group abundance can increase metal-binding sites, but higher pyrolysis temperature may reduce this abundance [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The chemistry also matters because different functional groups provide different binding modes. For example, surface complexation is a general mechanism that depends on reactive oxygen-containing groups, while electrostatic attraction depends on charge differences between the biochar surface and the metal ions [N2-R3]. The evidence also highlights that functional group density and accessibility can change with aging, increasing metal sorption capacity in some cases because of increased reactive surfaces and oxygenated functional groups [N6-R3][N3-F3].

The metal ions most strongly adsorbed are not uniformly predictable from the provided evidence, but several examples suggest a pattern. Cd is explicitly associated with precipitation, ion exchange, functional group complexation, and cation-π interactions [N2-R4]. Pb and Zn are also specifically mentioned in the aged-biochar evidence as metals whose sorption capacity can increase with aging [N3-F3]. The broader metal adsorption evidence supports the idea that adsorption strength varies by ion: some metals are better captured by electrostatic attraction, others by complexation, and still others by precipitation [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence does not provide a complete ranking of all metals, but it does indicate that metals such as Cd, Pb, Cu, and Zn are especially relevant in biochar applications [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5].

Aged biochar may shift adsorption behavior in both directions. The evidence indicates that aging can enhance metal sorption capacity for Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, Cu²⁺, and Zn²⁺ because of increased reactive surfaces, active sorption sites, and oxygenated functional groups [N3-F3]. However, it also notes that aging can reduce adsorption capacity for Cu(II) on aging rice husk biochar and that aging effects vary among metals, biochars, and soils [N3-F3]. A separate aging study similarly reports that aging could reverse biochar’s capacity for adsorbing cationic and anionic species, though it also suggests that some aging conditions can improve effectiveness for contaminants like TCIPP [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a nuanced view: aging can increase binding capacity for some metals and decrease it for others, depending on how the biochar’s functional groups and surface chemistry evolve [N3-F3][N6-R3].

Overall, the evidence suggests that biochar adsorption is a multi-pathway process, dominated by surface complexation, ion exchange, electrostatic attraction, and precipitation [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Functional group density and chemistry determine binding affinity and capacity, with oxygen-containing groups playing a central role [N1-R2]. The strongest adsorption responses are not uniform across all metals, and aged biochar can shift behavior in unpredictable ways depending on metal identity, aging history, and environmental conditions [N3-F3][N6-R3].

Biochar surface functional groups are dominated by oxygen-containing groups and aromatic structures, with the most commonly cited classes being carboxyl, phenolic, hydroxyl, and lactonic groups [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1]. The search evidence explicitly states that biochar surfaces contain abundant oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., carboxyl, phenolic, and hydroxyl groups) at relatively low temperatures [N1-R1]. Another source notes that biochar can be produced through pyrolysis with limited oxygen and that many organic groups are present [N1-R3]. The more detailed pyrolysis review also lists oxygen-containing carboxyl, phenolic, hydroxyl, and lactonic surface functional groups as relevant [N1-R4]. In addition, the review on functional groups explicitly frames the topic around oxygen-containing functional groups (OCFGs) and their formation, detection, and engineering [N1-R2]. Taken together, the evidence supports a strong conclusion: the dominant surface functional groups on biochar are oxygen-containing groups, with carboxyl, phenolic, hydroxyl, and lactonic groups being the most common [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R2].

Pyrolysis temperature has a clear effect on group abundance and distribution. At relatively low temperatures (300–500 °C), biochars typically retain a higher abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups [N1-F1]. As temperature increases, the abundance of acidic surface functional groups such as carboxyl and phenolic groups decreases, while basic functional groups increase [N1-F1]. The pyrolysis review also notes that at intermediate temperatures (500–700 °C), devolatilization promotes porosity and surface area development, and at higher temperatures (>700 °C), further aromatization and structural rearrangements may occur [N1-F1]. This implies that pyrolysis temperature controls the balance between oxygen-rich functional groups and aromatic carbon structures: lower temperature preserves more oxygen-containing groups, while higher temperature reduces them and increases aromatization [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Feedstock composition determines the functional group profile. The search evidence states that biochar adsorption performance is strongly correlated with the diversity and abundance of surface oxygen-containing functional groups, particularly [N1-R2], and the pyrolysis review notes that feedstock composition affects surface chemistry and overall material performance [N1-F1]. The separate feedstock-and-pyrolysis study further identifies pyrolysis temperature, H/C ratio, specific surface area, and ash fraction as dominant parameters affecting functional group signals [N5-F4]. This means that the same feedstock can yield different functional group profiles depending on pyrolysis conditions, and that feedstock composition shapes the initial pool of oxygen-containing and aromatic groups available for preservation or transformation during pyrolysis [N1-F1][N1-R2][N5-F4].

Aging or field exposure changes functional groups and metal-binding capacity. The evidence indicates that aging can increase metal sorption capacity for Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, Cu²⁺, and Zn²⁺ because of increased reactive surfaces, active sorption sites, and oxygenated functional groups [N3-F3]. A separate aging study reports that aging can reverse biochar’s capacity for adsorbing cationic and anionic species, though it also notes that some aging conditions can improve effectiveness [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Field aging is further described as a process that may involve freeze-thaw cycles, wetting-drying cycles, biotic and abiotic redox reactions, solubilization, and interactions with microbes and minerals, which can change physicochemical properties such as functional group content and ion exchange capacity [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that aging and field exposure can both increase and decrease biochar’s metal-binding capacity, depending on the specific aging mechanism and environmental context [N3-F3][N6-R3].

Overall, biochar is dominated by oxygen-containing functional groups such as carboxyl, phenolic, hydroxyl, and lactonic groups, with aromatic structures also present [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R2]. Pyrolysis temperature reduces oxygen-containing groups and increases aromatization at higher temperatures, while feedstock composition influences the initial functional group profile [N1-F1][N1-R2][N5-F4]. Aging and field exposure can alter functional groups and metal-binding capacity, sometimes increasing and sometimes decreasing it depending on the metal and environmental conditions [N3-F3][N6-R3].

Biochar immobilizes heavy metals in soils through several soil processes, with pH changes, precipitation, complexation, and organic-metal bonds being the most directly supported mechanisms. The field study explicitly states that biochar immobilizes metals by increasing soil pH, which causes metal precipitation as metal oxi-hydroxides [N3-R2]. It also notes that biochar-based remediation involves alkalinity, ash content, porous structure, and surface functional groups, and that aging can change physicochemical properties such as ion exchange capacity and aromaticity [N3-F3]. A broader biochar-remediation review similarly emphasizes that biochar can immobilize metals by increasing soil pH and that cation exchange, physical interactions, and other mechanisms are involved [N3-R2]. Taken together, the evidence supports a multi-pathway immobilization mechanism: biochar can raise soil pH to promote metal precipitation, provide surface sites for complexation, and alter redox conditions to influence metal speciation [N3-R2][N3-F3].

The evidence also supports the idea that biochar alters soil redox conditions and metal speciation. Biochar aging is described as involving biotic and abiotic redox reactions, solubilization, and interactions with microbes and minerals, which can change physicochemical properties and thus influence metal behavior [N3-F3]. The field study further notes that soil properties such as pH and dissolved organic matter (DOC) may change over time due to acid rain, plant roots, and microbial activity, affecting the availability of immobilized metals [N3-F3]. This indicates that biochar does not simply passively adsorb metals; it can actively shift the chemical environment around metals, altering their redox state and speciation [N3-F3][N3-R2].

The evidence for long-term immobilization versus temporary adsorption is mixed but generally leans toward partial long-term stabilization. The field study says that biochar may suffer long-term changes in physicochemical properties, including functional group content and ion exchange capacity, and that aging may enhance or decrease adsorption depending on the metal and conditions [N3-F3]. It also states that field aging can increase metal sorption capacity for Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, Cu²⁺, and Zn²⁺ because of increased reactive surfaces and oxygenated functional groups, but that other studies have reported the opposite effect [N3-F3]. The same study emphasizes that the stability of immobilized metals needs further exploration, especially desorption risk under long-term field conditions [N3-F3]. This suggests that biochar can provide both short-term adsorption and longer-term immobilization, but the duration and strength of immobilization depend on aging, soil conditions, and metal identity [N3-F3].

Field conditions and aging influence immobilization in several ways. The evidence indicates that field aging can enhance metal sorption for some metals, while weakening it for others, and that aging effects vary with metal, biochar, and soil [N3-F3]. Aging is also described as involving freeze-thaw cycles, wetting-drying cycles, biotic and abiotic redox reactions, and interactions with microbes and minerals, which can change physicochemical properties such as specific surface area, acidity, elemental composition, functional group, ion exchange capacity, and aromaticity [N3-F3]. A separate aging study reports that natural aging can enhance biochar’s adsorption capacity for some contaminants and that simulated aging may differ from natural aging because multiple environmental factors affect the aging process [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Taken together, these findings show that immobilization is not fixed at application; it evolves with field exposure and aging [N3-F3][N6-R3].

Overall, biochar immobilizes heavy metals through pH changes, precipitation, complexation, and organic-metal bonds, while also altering soil redox conditions and metal speciation [N3-R2][N3-F3]. The evidence supports both short-term adsorption and longer-term stabilization, but long-term immobilization is not guaranteed and depends on aging, soil properties, and metal identity [N3-F3]. Field conditions and aging can enhance or weaken immobilization, making the practical outcome highly context-dependent [N3-F3][N6-R3].

Pyrolysis conditions and feedstock choices strongly determine biochar’s functional groups and metal uptake. The evidence shows that biochar adsorption performance is strongly correlated with the diversity and abundance of surface oxygen-containing functional groups, particularly [N1-R2]. At relatively low temperatures, biochars retain a higher abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups, while higher temperatures reduce acidic functional groups and increase basic functional groups [N1-F1]. The pyrolysis review also notes that feedstock composition affects surface chemistry and overall material performance [N1-F1]. A feedstock-and-pyrolysis study further identifies pyrolysis temperature, H/C ratio, specific surface area, and ash fraction as dominant parameters affecting functional group signals [N5-F4]. Together, these sources support a clear conclusion: lower pyrolysis temperatures preserve more oxygen-containing groups and improve adsorption potential, while higher temperatures reduce oxygen-containing groups and increase aromatization, which can shift the balance from adsorption-relevant chemistry to more aromatic carbon [N1-F1][N1-R2][N5-F4].

Which conditions optimize adsorption versus immobilization depends on the application. For adsorption, the evidence suggests that lower-temperature biochars are advantageous because they retain more oxygen-containing functional groups, which are central to surface complexation and ion exchange [N1-R2][N1-F1]. However, for immobilization, the evidence points to biochar’s ability to raise soil pH and promote metal precipitation as metal oxi-hydroxides [N3-R2]. It also notes that biochar can alter soil redox conditions and metal speciation, which can stabilize metals over time [N3-F3]. In other words, adsorption is often driven by surface chemistry and functional group density, whereas immobilization is driven by pH changes, precipitation, and soil chemistry [N1-R2][N3-R2]. The evidence therefore supports a trade-off: lower temperatures may optimize adsorption, but higher temperatures may improve structural properties that support immobilization through pH effects and redox changes [N1-F1][N3-R2].

Trade-offs between cost, reactivity, and environmental impact are also evident. ## Integrated explanation: how surface functional groups affect metal-ion adsorption and heavy-metal immobilization in soils

Biochar’s effectiveness in removing metal ions and immobilizing heavy metals in soils depends fundamentally on its surface functional groups. The evidence shows that these groups are the chemical “handles” by which biochar interacts with metals: they determine adsorption mechanisms, binding strength, and the conditions under which metals remain bound in soil. The overall picture is one of multiple interacting processes, where pyrolysis conditions and feedstock composition shape the functional group profile, aging and field exposure reshape it further, and soil chemistry governs whether metals are temporarily adsorbed or more permanently immobilized [N1-R2][N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R2].

### 1) Which functional groups dominate biochar, and how they form during pyrolysis

Biochar is dominated by **oxygen-containing functional groups** and **aromatic structures**. The most commonly cited groups are **carboxyl, phenolic, hydroxyl, and lactonic groups**, with other oxygen-containing heteroatoms also present [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-F1]. The review evidence explicitly states that biochar surfaces contain abundant oxygen-containing functional groups (e.g., carboxyl, phenolic, and hydroxyl groups) at relatively low temperatures [N1-R1], and that biochar can be produced through pyrolysis with limited oxygen and that many organic groups are present [N1-R3]. A more detailed review also lists **oxygen-containing carboxyl, phenolic, hydroxyl, and lactonic surface functional groups** as relevant [N1-R4]. Taken together, these sources support a clear conclusion: biochar is chemically heterogeneous, but oxygen-containing groups are the most commonly recognized and functionally important classes [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R2].

Pyrolysis temperature strongly controls group abundance and distribution. At relatively low temperatures (300–500 °C), biochars typically retain a higher abundance of oxygen-containing functional groups [N1-F1]. As temperature increases, the abundance of acidic surface functional groups such as carboxyl and phenolic groups decreases, while basic functional groups increase [N1-F1]. The pyrolysis review also notes that intermediate temperatures (500–700 °C) promote porosity and surface area development, and that higher temperatures (>700 °C) may lead to further aromatization and structural rearrangements [N1-F1]. This means that pyrolysis temperature acts as a tuning knob: lower temperature preserves more oxygen-containing groups, while higher temperature reduces them and increases aromaticity [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Feedstock composition determines the functional group profile. The evidence indicates that biochar adsorption performance is strongly correlated with the diversity and abundance of surface oxygen-containing functional groups, particularly [N1-R2]. It also states that feedstock composition affects surface chemistry and overall material performance [N1-F1]. A separate feedstock-and-pyrolysis study identifies pyrolysis temperature, H/C ratio, specific surface area, and ash fraction as dominant parameters affecting functional group signals [N5-F4]. This means that the same feedstock can yield different functional group profiles depending on pyrolysis conditions, and that feedstock composition shapes the initial pool of oxygen-containing and aromatic groups available for preservation or transformation during pyrolysis [N1-F1][N1-R2][N5-F4].

Aging or field exposure changes functional groups and metal-binding capacity. The evidence indicates that aging can increase metal sorption capacity for Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, Cu²⁺, and Zn²⁺ because of increased reactive surfaces, active sorption sites, and oxygenated functional groups [N3-F3]. A separate aging study reports that aging can reverse biochar’s capacity for adsorbing cationic and anionic species, though it also notes that some aging conditions can improve effectiveness [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Field aging is further described as a process involving freeze-thaw cycles, wetting-drying cycles, biotic and abiotic redox reactions, solubilization, and interactions with microbes and minerals, which can change physicochemical properties such as functional group content and ion exchange capacity [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that aging and field exposure can both increase and decrease biochar’s metal-binding capacity, depending on the specific aging mechanism and environmental context [N3-F3][N6-R3].

### 2) How these functional groups enable metal-ion adsorption

The functional groups on biochar do not act as a single mechanism; instead, they enable a combination of adsorption pathways. The strongest evidence points to **surface complexation**, **ion exchange**, **electrostatic attraction**, and **surface precipitation** [N2-R3][N2-R1][N2-R4]. A broader review explicitly lists major physicochemical sorption processes as surface sorption, electrostatic attraction, surface complexation, precipitation, and ion exchange [N2-R3]. Another source expands this by mentioning adsorption mechanisms including pore filling, electrostatic adsorption, π–π interactions, ion exchange, and mineral formation [N2-R1]. A Cd-specific example also points to precipitation, ion exchange, functional group complexation, and cation-π interactions [N2-R4]. Taken together, these sources support a multi-pathway view of biochar adsorption: metals are captured through multiple mechanisms, and the dominant ones are surface complexation, ion exchange, electrostatic attraction, and precipitation [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

Functional group density and chemistry strongly influence binding affinity and capacity. The evidence states that biochar adsorption performance is strongly correlated with the diversity and abundance of surface oxygen-containing functional groups, particularly [N1-R2]. The pyrolysis review also notes that acidic surface functional groups such as carboxyl and phenolic groups decrease with increasing temperature, while basic functional groups increase [N1-F1]. The evidence indicates that aging can enhance metal sorption capacity for Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, Cu²⁺, and Zn²⁺ because of increased reactive surfaces, active sorption sites, and oxygenated functional groups [N3-F3]. Taken together, the evidence supports a nuanced view: aging can increase binding capacity for some metals and decrease it for others, depending on metal identity, aging history, and environmental conditions [N3-F3][N6-R3].

The field study explicitly states that biochar immobilizes metals by increasing soil pH, which causes metal precipitation as metal oxi-hydroxides [N3-R2]. It also notes that biochar-based remediation involves alkalinity, ash content, porous structure, and surface functional groups, and that aging can change physicochemical properties such as ion exchange capacity and aromaticity [N3-F3]. A broader biochar-remediation review similarly emphasizes that biochar can immobilize metals by increasing soil pH and that cation exchange, physical interactions, and other mechanisms are involved [N3-R2]. Taken together, the evidence supports a multi-pathway immobilization mechanism: biochar can raise soil pH to promote metal precipitation, provide surface sites for complexation, and alter redox conditions to influence metal speciation [N3-R2][N3-F3].

The evidence also supports the idea that biochar alters soil redox conditions and metal speciation. Biochar aging is described as involving biotic and abiotic redox reactions, solubilization, and interactions with microbes and minerals, which can change physicochemical properties and thus influence metal behavior [N3-F3]. The field study further notes that soil properties such as pH and dissolved organic matter (DOC) may change over time due to acid rain, plant roots, and microbial activity, affecting the availability of immobilized metals [N3-F3]. Pyrolysis conditions and feedstock choices strongly determine biochar’s functional groups and metal uptake. It also notes that biochar can alter soil redox conditions and metal speciation, which can stabilize metals over time [N3-F3]. In other words, adsorption is often driven by surface chemistry and functional group density, whereas immobilization is driven by pH changes, precipitation, and soil chemistry [N1-R2][N3-R2]. The evidence therefore supports a trade-off: lower temperatures may optimize adsorption, but higher temperatures may improve structural properties that support immobilization through pH effects and redox changes [N1-F1][N3-R2].

Trade-offs between cost, reactivity, and environmental impact are also evident. Lower pyrolysis temperatures can increase oxygen-containing groups and adsorption capacity, but may require more feedstock or different handling conditions. Higher temperatures can reduce oxygen-containing groups and increase aromatization, which may lower adsorption but improve long-term structural stability [N1-F1].
